turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Morning. I'll grab a blood pressure before you go in. One thirty-eight over eighty-six, pulse seventy-six. All pretty ordinary.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Good. Can we get on with it? I've got work.
[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Doctor's free now. Oh, your partner rang yesterday about the snoring and you being wrecked tired. I popped it on the note.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Course he did. He's dramatic. I snore a bit, everyone does. I'm not tired.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come in, take a seat. I'm Dr Nguyen. Headaches are on the note from your usual GP, but tell me in your own words.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Same headaches I've always had. He booked this, I didn't. It's hardly an emergency.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long is always?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Years. Um, since before the lockdowns, or around then. I can't put a year on it.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Where do you feel them?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Right side, mostly. Throbs if I ignore it. Behind the eye sometimes. Ordinary migraine stuff.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Did someone actually call it migraine?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, years back. Classic migraine. I don't need that dug up again.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): What do you take when one hits?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Sumatriptan. Fifty milligram tablets. And Panadol.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): How many sumatriptan in a week, roughly?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Not many. Well, a few times a week, if I'm honest. I don't sit there counting.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the Panadol — strength, and how often?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): The usual ones, two tablets, most days, sometimes again in the arvo. It's only paracetamol.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): So paracetamol, two five-hundred milligram tablets, a gram, most days, and some days a second gram?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, alright, if you want it in numbers. I skip plenty of days too. Don't write it like I'm hooked.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any other regular medicines?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I tried those magnesium tablets from the chemist. Stopped them. Waste of money.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): When did you stop the magnesium?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Months ago. Don't ask me which month.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure tablets, antidepressants, anything like that?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing. I'm not on a pile of scripts.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does the pain wake you out of sleep, or is it there when the alarm goes?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): It's just there in the morning sometimes. Doesn't wake me. I get up and it eases. Same old.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any weakness, numbness, trouble getting words out, or vision going funny?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None of that. I'd notice.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fever, a stiff neck, or a headache that explodes out of nowhere?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no, and no. They're annoying, not scary.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Quick look, then. Straight ahead for me. Pupils are equal and they react to light. No facial droop. Push up on my hands — power's equal in both arms.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): See? Normal. I said it was nothing.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Finger to nose is accurate, and you walked in steadily. Neck's soft, no stiffness. No focal sign I can find.

[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me play it back. Years of right-sided throbbing headache labelled migraine, sumatriptan fifty milligrams a few times a week, paracetamol a gram most days and sometimes twice, nothing you've described as a red flag, exam clear. Partner's on about snoring, which you reckon is overblown, and you're not tired.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the size of it. Are we done?

[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): My plan was to skip a scan. This sits more with medication overuse on top of migraine than with something structural. Ease off the Panadol and the triptan, and we'd only look again in a month if you were still bothered.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine by me. Scans are a hassle anyway.

[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, the mornings — I should say, since he made me promise. A few mornings I actually vomited, and it's worse before I get up, not like the old ones. But it's settled, not this week.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): You vomited. That's new, and you didn't put it up front. How many times?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Twice. Maybe three. Hardly a pattern.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): When did this morning pattern start?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Last winter, or the one before — no, hang on, that's the old headaches. This morning thing is, um, a few weeks? A month? I genuinely can't date it.
[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any change in your vision with those morning ones?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Bit blurry, both eyes, for a few seconds when I first open them. That's sleep, not a stroke. Gone before I'm at the kettle.
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the snoring — has he seen you stop breathing?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): He says that. I don't buy it. I feel fine. I drive, I do a full day at the warehouse.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): Alright. That does shift me. I was happy with no imaging. I'm still not booking a CT today.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the morning headache or any vomiting hasn't settled in two weeks, we might organise a CT of the head. Not before that.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Might. So nothing's actually booked.
[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): Correct, nothing booked. Two weeks, though, I want to see you either way, and we decide then.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Even if I'm sweet?
[SEG0054] person_3 (DOCTOR): Even then. A planned visit, not a maybe. The scan is the maybe.
[SEG0055] person_3 (DOCTOR): Until then, paracetamol no more than two days in a week, and sumatriptan no more than two days in a week. More than that keeps the headache going.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll try. Not promising I'll be perfect. Work's flat out.
[SEG0057] person_3 (DOCTOR): If you get a sudden worst headache of your life, weakness, confusion, or you can't keep fluids down, don't wait out the two weeks. That's an emergency department visit.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, yeah. Not going to happen.

[SEG0059] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm not making a new diagnosis today. Working impression is still migraine with possible medication overuse, and I can't exclude a secondary cause for that new morning pattern until we see how it behaves.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Secondary. You mean a tumour. Just say it.
[SEG0061] person_3 (DOCTOR): I mean I don't know yet. A tumour is one of several unlikely things a scan would look for, only if this doesn't settle. I'm not saying you have one.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. Good.
[SEG0063] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Knock knock. Do you need a request form printed, or a review booked?
[SEG0064] person_3 (DOCTOR): No request form. Please book a review in two weeks. Routine, not urgent.
[SEG0065] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Two weeks... Friday morning's open, or the Thursday arvo.
[SEG0066] person_2 (PATIENT): Friday. I can still make the early shift if it's first up.
[SEG0067] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): First one, eight-fifteen, Friday fortnight. I'll text you a reminder.
[SEG0068] person_2 (PATIENT): Don't text him as well. He'll turn up and make a speech.
[SEG0069] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Just you. No worries.
[SEG0070] person_3 (DOCTOR): Anything you wanted to ask that we haven't touched?
[SEG0071] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I'll ease off the tablets. Don't make a big deal out of two vomits.

spec.situation: Person with long headaches who now has a different pattern (worse in the morning, or with vomiting); takes sumatriptan or paracetamol often; partner says snoring and tiredness too; patient dismisses it. Doctor does a quick neuro exam and orders a scan conditionally.
features: doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.
vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.

bad.reason: Snoring supported, but 'mild' severity is not stated.
bad.text: Snoring (category=respiratory, status=present, severity=mild, temporality=current, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

omissions.text: Headache is sometimes behind the right eye.
Negative finding asked and answered: no vision going funny before later clarification of brief bilateral blurring on waking with the morning headaches.
Paracetamol details are incomplete: patient said the 'usual' tablets are two 500 mg tablets, most days, sometimes a second dose in the afternoon, and that he skips plenty of days too.
No other regular medicines, specifically no blood pressure tablets or antidepressants.
Magnesium was an over-the-counter chemist product and was stopped because it was a 'waste of money'; stopped months ago.
Morning headaches were present on waking/alarm and eased after getting up.
Neck examination finding also included 'neck soft' in addition to no stiffness.
The partner had reported snoring and that the patient was 'wrecked tired', but the patient denied being tired.
Possible sleep apnoea concern was raised by partner reporting witnessed breathing pauses during sleep; the patient disputed this rather than simply denying it.
Recorded symptom status is wrong: the brief blurring in both eyes was described only with those morning headaches and gone within seconds on waking, not an ongoing current symptom.
Doctor explicitly decided not to book a CT head today, and after the new history still said no CT was booked now.
Follow-up plan was stronger than a generic planned review: doctor wanted to see the patient in two weeks either way, even if asymptomatic; the scan was the only conditional part.
Review was actually scheduled for Friday fortnight at 8:15 am, routine/not urgent, with a text reminder to the patient only.

Real concern/disagreement: patient pressed 'You mean a tumour', and doctor clarified that tumour was only one of several unlikely possibilities a scan would look for and he was not saying the patient had one.
